1	# Per-paper extraction instructions, v6 (GP-RareLink; Claude Code route, D-20)

3	*Changes from v2 come from the Stage 3 findings (`reports/poc_stage3_findings.md`) and decision D-22, marked "(v3)". Changes from v3 come from the Stage 3b findings (`reports/poc_stage3b_findings.md`) and decisions D-23 and D-24, marked "(v4)". The change from v5 is D-31 (Jimmy, 2026-10-19), from the re-audit (`reports/poc_stage4_5_findings.md` §10.7), marked "(v6)": no positional reading of stacked cells. v6 is the candidate for the frozen pipeline; it has not been run.*
4	
5	You extract structured evidence from **one** published paper for a literature-curation study of A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20), the disease caused by germline *TNFAIP3* variants. Your output is checked by script (every quote must be found verbatim in the paper) and then by a separate reviewer, so accuracy and honest abstention matter more than completeness.
6	
7	## Inputs (paths are given in your task)
8	
9	1. **The paper**: a Markdown file converted from the PMC or Europe PMC full text. Its first lines give the PMID and title. Merged table cells are repeated in every row and column they cover.
10	   - **(v3)** The file may end with a `## Supplementary material` section converted from the files published with the article. Treat it as part of the paper and quote it verbatim like any other text.
11	   - Some supplementary files are excerpts, with `[...]` marking omitted lines. Never join text across `[...]`.
12	   - **(v4)** In tables converted from supplementary files, ` / ` separates values that were stacked on separate lines inside one cell (see "Stacked cells" below; changed in v6).
13	2. **The schema**: `pipeline/extract/claude_code/schema_ha20_v5.json`. It defines five tables, their fields, types, allowed values, and a description for each.
14	3. **The rules**: `pipeline/extract/sliders_adapter/prompts/extraction_rules_v1.md`. Apply all nine. Where this file is more specific (scope, labels, table symbols), this file wins.
15	
16	**What you may read.** Read only these three files.
17	- Do not open any other file in the repository.
18	- Do not use web search or web fetch.
19	- Do not use anything you remember about this paper, its authors, its patients, the gene or the variants.
20	
21	**What counts as missing.** If the paper doesn't say it, the value is missing (see "Values" below).
22	
23	## Scope: who gets a row (v3, D-22)
24	
25	- **In scope:**
26	  - every person the paper describes who has a *TNFAIP3* variant or an HA20 (A20 haploinsufficiency) diagnosis;
27	  - relatives the paper describes in relation to such a person, whether tested (including tested negative) or affected.
28	- **Out of scope:** other members of a cohort, for example patients whose variants are in other genes, or who have no variant. They get **no** rows. Record the study's total number of patients, as the authors state it, in `publications.cohort_size_as_stated`.
29	- **People from summaries of earlier reports are in scope** when they meet the rule above: a literature table in a case report, or a review describing individuals. Each gets its own row, with `source_reference_in_review` filled verbatim.
30	  - **(v4)** A previously published person mentioned only in passing (for example one sentence in the Discussion) is in scope only when the paper gives at least one individual-level fact about that person beyond the diagnosis: sex, age, variant or a feature.
31	  - **(v4, D-23)** When a table has a per-patient reference or source column, copy that cell into `source_reference_in_review` for each patient, also in cohort and survey papers. Do not leave it only in `method_note`; the cross-paper merge depends on it.
32	- **Variants in other genes:**
33	  - record one only for an in-scope person, and only when the paper attributes it to that person unambiguously;
34	  - do not list risk alleles or polygenic-score variants;
35	  - **(v4)** do not create a row for a variant the paper names but does not describe (no printed variant), for example "variants in PIK3R1 and HBB";
36	  - if the attribution is contradictory, leave it out and say so in `method_note`.
37	- **(v4) Other variant rows to leave out:** common variants the authors dismiss as non-causal (for example a frequent SNP they call benign), and variants found only in tumour tissue (somatic).
38	- **(v4) Mosaic carriers:** a person with a germline mosaic *TNFAIP3* variant is in scope; record zygosity `mosaic`.
39	- **`reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant`** is `true` only when the paper describes at least one identifiable in-scope person, that is, with any individual-level detail. A paper that mentions such patients only as counts or at group level gets `false`.
40	
41	## Labels (v3, D-22)
42	
43	Choose each person's `individual_label_in_paper` by the first rule that applies, so that two independent extractions give the same label:
44	1. **The paper's own label**, verbatim, in the form it uses most often (e.g. `P1`, `Patient 3`, `II-2`).
45	2. **A relative without an own label:** `<relation as written> of <label of the related person>` (e.g. `mother of P1`, `sister of patient`).
46	3. **A table row without a label column:** `Table <n> row <k>`, with k counting data rows from the top (e.g. `Table 2 row 3`).
47	4. **A previously published person described in the text without a label:** `ref <reference as printed> patient` (e.g. `ref [12] patient`). Add ` 2`, ` 3` for further people from the same reference, in order of mention.
48	5. **The single unnamed patient of a case report:** `patient`.
49	6. **Otherwise:** `unnamed person <k>`, in order of first mention.
50	
51	**(v4) Additions:**
52	- **Patients as table columns:** `Table <n> column <k>`, with k counting data columns from the left.
53	- **A table column of bare numbers that index the patients** (values like 1, 2, 3 under a heading such as "No.", "Case" or "Patient number"): `Table <n> #<value>` (e.g. `Table 3 #1`). If the values are labels such as "P1" or "Case 2", or the text uses its own label for that person, rule 1 applies.
54	- **The same label in two families** (e.g. two people called "IV:1"): `<label> (Family <n>)`.
55	- **Role words are not labels.** "The proband", "the index case" or "our patient" do not count as the paper's own label; use rule 5 or 6.
56	- **Relatives without a stated sex:** when the paper says only "parents", "children" or "siblings", write `parent of X`, `child of X` or `sibling of X` (and `parent of X 2` for the second). Never guess "mother" or "brother".
57	- A made-up label (rules 3–6) still needs a span: quote the text where the person first appears.
58	
59	Use the identical label in every table for the same person.
60	
61	## Output: one JSON file, at the path given in your task
62	
63	```json
64	{
65	  "pmid": "<from the paper's header line>",
66	  "instructions_version": "extract_v6",
67	  "reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant": true,
68	  "relevance_note": "<one sentence, with a short quote, saying why>",
69	  "method_note": "<how you worked, e.g. whether a script transcribed a table; list any contradictions you found in the paper>",
70	  "tables": {
71	    "publications": [ROW],
72	    "individuals": [ROW, ...],
73	    "variants": [ROW, ...],
74	    "phenotypic_features": [ROW, ...],
75	    "phenotype_checklist": [ROW, ...]
76	  }
77	}
78	```
79	
80	A **ROW** is an object with every field of that table, using the field names exactly as in the schema. Each field maps to a **cell**:
81	
82	```json
83	{"value": <value>, "span": "<exact quote from the paper>"}
84	```
85	
86	### Values
87	- **Type.** Use the schema's type for each field. Enum fields take only the listed strings.
88	- **Missing values.** Follow each field's schema description.
89	  - Where the description says "null", use `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
90	  - Otherwise, text and enum fields take `{"value": "not reported", "span": null}`, and numeric, date and boolean fields take `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
91	- **`pmid` fields.** The value comes from the header line; the span is that header line, e.g. `"PMID: 12345678"`.
92	- **`*_iso8601` fields.** These are your conversion of the matching original-text field. Give them only when the original text states a number, and use the same span as the original-text field.
93	- **`hpo_label_candidate` and `hpo_id_candidate`.** These are your suggestions. Give an ID only if you are sure of it; otherwise null. Their span is `null`.
94	- **`checklist_feature`.** The span is `null`, because the names come from the schema.
95	- **Age at diagnosis.** Record it in `age_at_diagnosis_*`. Don't put it in onset or last evaluation.
96	
97	### Spans
98	- **Every non-missing value needs a span**, except the fields listed just above.
99	- **Copy exactly.** A span is copied character for character from the paper Markdown, including unusual spaces and symbols. Never paraphrase, correct or join text that isn't contiguous.
100	- **Keep it short.** Use the smallest sentence fragment, table cell or table-row segment that supports the value. That is normally under 300 characters.
101	- **Tables with patients as rows.** Quote a contiguous piece of the row from the patient label through the cell.
102	- **Tables with patients as columns.** Quote the row from its row label through that patient's cell, e.g. `| Sex | F | M` for the second patient column. Name the column header once in `method_note`.
103	- **Multiple places.** If support sits in several places, `span` may be a list of exact quotes:
104	  - up to **five** for `treatment_summary`, `functional_evidence_statement`, `parental_testing_statement` and `clinical_diagnosis_basis`;
105	  - up to **three** for any other field.
106	
107	### Rows
108	- **`publications`:** exactly one row for this paper.
109	- **`individuals`:** one row per in-scope person (see Scope), labelled by the Labels rules.
110	- **`variants`:** one row per (person, variant).
111	  - `variant_original_string` is the **shortest** contiguous text giving the variant, not a whole sentence. Put the transcript, cDNA and protein parts in their own fields.
112	  - **(v3)** If the paper ties a *TNFAIP3* variant to the person but prints no variant description (only in a figure or an unavailable supplement), keep the row with `variant_original_string` = `"not reported"`. Never fill it from memory.
113	- **`phenotypic_features`:** one row per feature the paper explicitly reports present (`observed`) or explicitly reports absent (`excluded`) for that person. No rows for features the paper doesn't mention.
114	- **`phenotype_checklist`:** for **every** individual, one row for **each** of the 20 checklist features in the schema's description of that table, using the names exactly as listed there. Status is `observed`, `excluded` or `not reported` under rule 4.
115	
116	### Absence and evidence basis (D-21, D-22)
117	- **`evidence_basis` is required** on every `phenotypic_features` row, and on every checklist row whose status is not `not reported`.
118	- **Group statements.** You may mark a feature `excluded` for a person from a statement about a group **only when the statement names the group explicitly**, e.g. "only Pt3 of the four patients had recurrent fevers". Such rows take `evidence_basis = "inferred from group statement"`.
119	  - Counts without names ("arthritis in 2/4") do not exclude anyone.
120	- **(v3) Table symbols.** A `-`, `–`, `0`, `N` or similar cell counts as `excluded` only when the paper's legend or text defines that symbol as absent or negative.
121	  - Quote that definition as a second span next to the cell.
122	  - Otherwise the cell is `not reported` (rule 6). Empty cells, `NA` and `ND` are always `not reported`.
123	- **(v3) Study criteria are not evidence.** Never use a study's inclusion or exclusion criteria (e.g. "patients with malignancy were excluded") to mark a feature for a person.
124	- **Narrow and broad features.** A narrower absence never excludes a broader checklist item. "No arthritis" does not exclude "arthritis or arthralgia"; leave that item `not reported` unless arthralgia is also addressed. The same applies to other composite items, e.g. "skin lesions (rash, folliculitis, erythema nodosum)".
125	- **(v5, D-27) Normal findings.** When the paper reports a finding as normal or negative for a person ("CRP was normal", "normal C3 and C4 levels", "ANA negative"), record the abnormality it rules out as the feature and mark it `excluded`: `feature_text_as_stated` = "elevated CRP", "low complement", "positive ANA". Keep the paper's own words in the span ("CRP was normal"). Name only an abnormality the finding measures; a normal examination or investigation as a whole ("gastrointestinal investigation was negative") excludes nothing more specific than what it names, so write it as the paper does and say so in `method_note`.
126	- **(v4) Zero counts.** A count of 0 in a table of counts (e.g. "0" or "0/2" in a column for a disease group) excludes no one, like any count without names. Text that names the group ("none of the patients had uveitis") still excludes.
127	- **(v6, D-31) Stacked cells.** A cell with several values separated by ` / ` lists values that were stacked on separate lines (often one per patient). **Do not assign them to people by position**, even when the number of values equals the number of people. Use a stacked value for a person only when the paper labels it for that person (for example "P1: 18 / P2: 24", or a sentence naming the person and the value). Otherwise record the field or checklist item as `not reported` for each person in that row, and say in `method_note` which table and columns were stacked. A value the same for every person in the row, printed once (not stacked), is not affected.
128	- **Contradictions inside the paper.** If the paper says both that a person has a feature and that they don't:
129	  - emit both `phenotypic_features` rows, each with its own span;
130	  - set that checklist item to `not reported`;
131	  - list the contradiction in `method_note`.
132	
133	### Variant fields belong to this person's variant (v5, D-29)
134	Zygosity, inheritance, variant type, pathogenicity, ACMG criteria and functional evidence describe **one person's variant**. Fill them only from:
135	- this person's own table row or column, or a sentence that names this person or this exact variant; or
136	- a statement about a **named group that includes this person** and gives one value for all of them ("all six patients carried heterozygous variants").
137	
138	Leave the field `not reported` (with span null) when:
139	- the statement is about the cohort's or the paper's variants in general, without naming a group this person is clearly in ("the variants were classified as pathogenic");
140	- the statement lists several values for a group ("splice-site, frameshift and nonsense variants"): it does not say which one is this person's;
141	- the paper gives this person a different or open status elsewhere: a variant not identified or not determined, a mosaic or somatic finding, a VUS, a relative not tested. A group statement never overrides that;
142	- the value is about another person's variant, for example a relative carrying the proband's variant, unless the paper says it for the relative.
143	
144	Variant type: record only a class the paper states for this variant (or for a named group of variants that includes it). Do not derive it from the HGVS string.
145	
146	### Inheritance (v4, D-24)
147	- **De novo:** only when the paper states parental testing with the variant absent in both parents (rule 8).
148	- **Inherited:** record `inherited maternal` or `inherited paternal` when the paper states that the named parent carries the same variant, even if it never uses the word "inherited". Quote that statement in `parental_testing_statement`. Use `inherited unspecified parent` when it says a parent carries it without saying which.
149	- **Otherwise:** `not reported`. Do not infer from a pedigree drawing or from an affected but untested parent.
150	- This is more specific than rule 8, so it wins.
151	
152	### When the paper describes no in-scope person
153	For example, a review without patient-level detail, or a paper about something else:
154	- set `reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant` to `false`;
155	- fill the `publications` row;
156	- leave the other tables empty.
157	
158	### Large papers
159	If the output is long, you may build it in parts with a short Python script and combine the parts.
160	- Every value must still come from your reading of the paper.
161	- If a script transcribes a table, check its output against the table and say so in `method_note`.
162	- Use only your own scratch directory (given in your task) for temporary files.
163	
164	## Finish
165	1. Validate that your file parses as JSON.
166	2. Check every span occurs verbatim in the paper.
167	3. Check every row has every schema field.
168	4. Reply with:
169	   - the number of rows per table;
170	   - the number of individuals;
171	   - anything you were unsure how to record.

12	AbstractCase PresentationA 3-year-and-6-month-old child was reported to have recurrent high fever with generalized lymph node enlargement and significant elevation of inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein and procalcitonin in tests. Later, whole exome sequencing determined that the child's disease was haploinsufficiency of A20 (HA20).ResultsAfter immunosuppressive therapy, the child's symptoms improved significantly, and the inflammatory markers dropped to the normal range.ConclusionBecause of the characteristics of HA20, this disease is often underdiagnosed and misdiagnosed in clinical practice. 14	## Introduction
15	
16	Haploinsufficiency of A20 (HA20) is a rare monogenic autoinflammatory disease, which was first reported and named by Zhou et al. in 2016 (1). A20, also called TNFα-induced protein 3 (TNFAIP3), is a protein including 790 amino acids coded by the TNFAIP3 gene, located on chromosome 6, which plays an important role in the negative regulation of inflammation and immunity. Loss of function mutation in TNFAIP3 gene leads to HA20 and to an autoinflammatory or autoimmune disease. HA20 has a clinical presentation similar to infectious diseases and common rheumatic immune diseases, but with significant heterogeneity, and the correct diagnosis is often not determined in a timely manner in clinical practice (1, 2). Especially in the early stage of the disease, it often presents with recurrent high fever, significantly elevated inflammatory indexes, and ineffective anti-infective treatment. It is easy to misdiagnose or miss the diagnosis, and the possibility of HA20 needs to be considered. We present the clinical features of a case of HA20 in a child admitted to the Department of Pediatric Cardiology of the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University, and conduct a literature review and discussion to improve the understanding of HA20 in clinical work.

51	## Case description
52	
53	A male child, 3 years and 6 months old, was admitted to our hospital for fever and multiple skin rashes throughout the body. The child presented with toothache and fever of 38°C 10 days ago. The fever persisted even after the toothache improved. The patient was treated with antibiotics for 3 days at the outpatient department, but the fever did not improve, and the fever peaks at 40.3°C with 4–5 h intervals between fever peaks. The child was found to be hyperopic at about 6 months of age and is currently farsighted with 6.75 diopters. The father had a previous “transsphenoidal pituitary adenomectomy” for “non-functional pituitary macroadenoma, hypopituitarism.” The mother has “Mediterranean anemia.”
54	
55	Physical examination at admission: lymphadenopathy was medium hard and movable in the neck, submandibular, and subchin bilaterally. Oral mucosa was smooth, pharynx was congested, tonsils were swollen (III°), and dental cavities were present. The spleen was palpable 1 cm below the ribs, medium in quality, and without percussion pain. The rest of the cardiopulmonary, abdominal, joint, and neurological examination showed no significant abnormality. The initial findings of the tests carried out after the child's admission to hospital are shown in Table 1 and Table 2.
56	
57	**Figure 1**: TNFAIP3 (chr6:138197151): NM_006290.3:c.653del:p.Leu218TrpfsTer10 sequencing results; red boxes are detection sites. In the picture, from top to bottom, are the first witness (A), the father of the first witness (B), and the mother of the first witness (C). The genetic test results indicate that the TNFAIP3 gene variant in this pediatric patient is from the father and is a heterozygous mutation.

70	The child was admitted to the hospital and given piperacillin sodium and tazobactam sodium for anti-infection due to the patient's infection indicators were well above normal. Seven days after the fever subsided, recurrent high fever with lethargy, oral and pendulous ulcers, generalized red maculopapular rash, and generalized superficial lymph node enlargement, liver, and spleen enlargement were seen again. The repeated blood test showed that C-reactive protein (CRP) was 108.66 mg/L, white blood cell count (WBC) was 9.56 × 10^9/L, neutrophil numerals (NEUT#) was 8.54 × 10^9/L, procalcitonin (PCT) was 127.00 ng/ml, lumbar puncture intracranial pressure was 155 mmH_2O, and cerebrospinal fluid tests were negative. The fever subsided after treatment with acyclovir, meropenem, fluconazole, and gamma globulin 2 g/kg, but later there was still recurrent low-grade fever and peeling of skin at the junction of perianal, finger and toe nails, recurrent oral ulcers, and repeatedly increased CRP. The child's symptoms and medical history suggested that there might be an acute immune response to connective tissue disease or viral infection; then, we perfected whole exome sequencing. In the meantime, due to the high likelihood of connective tissue disease, he was given prednisone treatment (1 mg/kg qd) and his recurrent fever improved, but he still had recurrent oral ulcers. Then, the prednisone dose was gradually reduced. Based on the results for the full exome, methotrexate (5 mg qw) and thalidomide (12.5 mg qd) were added, after which the child did not have any more oral ulcers. Then, the child is discharged from the hospital. After 1 month of treatment at home, he returned to the hospital for follow-up: CRP was 0.94 mg/L, WBC was 6.14 × 10^9/L, NEUT# was 3.85 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin was 102 g/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 40 mm/h; abdominal ultrasound showed multiple lymph nodes in the abdominal cavity and mesentery, smaller than before. Ten months later, we saw this child in our clinic and found that the patient did not develop recurrent fever and oral ulcers, and the blood test showed that CRP and PCT were reduced to normal, ESR fluctuated between 20 and 60 mm/h, and P-ANCA was still weakly positive.
71	
72	Whole exome sequencing revealed a heterozygous mutation in the affected TNFAIP3 gene, chr6: 138197151, NM_006290.3 c.653del p.Leu218TrpfsTer10, derived from the father, consistent with HA20. This child's grandparents tested negative for the gene, suggesting that the mutation came from the father. The shift variant is a 1-base pair deletion, resulting in an out-of-frame transcription product and an early termination codon that may cause protein truncation or activation of nonsense-mediated mRNA degradation, resulting in loss of function of the protein product of the TNFAIP3 gene. The downstream truncation variant of this variant is known to be pathogenic. The results are shown in the Figure 1.

74	## Literature review
75	
76	To understand patients with HA20 onset and diagnosis in childhood, we searched the PubMed database using the keywords “HA20” from the year of creation to June 2022 and limited the search language to English, and exclude patients with onset or diagnosis in adulthood and young adulthood by carefully reading.
77	
78	A total of 15 pediatric cases have been reported (Table 3). We further analyzed the data of these pediatric patients, including gender, age, and various common symptoms. Of these cases, six (40%) were male and nine (60%) were female. The number and percentage of these pediatric patients with various symptoms were as follows: nine (60%) had recurrent fever, nine (60%) had recurrent oral ulcers, four (26.6%) had recurrent genital ulcers, three (20%) had rashes, and six (40%) had arthritis. Most of these patients had different mutation sites in the TNFAIP3 gene, with a small number of patients having mutations at the same site. In terms of treatment, pharmacological treatment in these patients also varied. The commonly used drugs were colchicine, prednisolone, sirolimus, tacrolimus, and infliximab.

102	## Discussion
103	
104	The young pediatric patient presented with recurrent high fever at the onset of the disease, with a generalized rash and recurrent oral ulcers, significantly elevated CRP (up to 108.66 mg/L), PCT (up to 127 ng/ml), and other infection indicators, no special abnormalities in rheumatologic immune indicators on comprehensive examination, and no improvement after anti-infection treatment, which was finally diagnosed as HA20 after whole exome sequencing. Due to HA20 being difficult to differentiate from other diseases, it is often initially diagnosed as other connective tissue diseases such as juvenile idiopathic arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), Behcet's disease, and rheumatoid arthritis. In particular, HA20 is different in that it does not have specific abnormalities in rheumatologic immune indexes (13).
105	
106	In previous studies, elevated procalcitonin has been considered an important marker of bacterial infection in newborns and children, especially in febrile children without symptoms of local infection, which is why we made the diagnosis of infectious disease and administered antibiotics in this study (14). In healthy populations, circulating levels of PCT are usually below 0.1 ng/ml. In viral infections and inflammatory responses, PCT concentrations can increase to 1.5 ng/ml. In bacterial infections, PCT levels greater than 0.5 ng/ml are generally considered positive, and the highest levels may be >100,000 times the normal level. The highest value of PCT in this child was 127 ng/ml, which is well above the diagnostic range. Moreover, if the elevation of procalcitonin is due to bacterial infection, it will decrease rapidly after targeted antibiotic treatment; as described previously, the children in this study did not have a significant decrease in procalcitonin levels after antibiotic treatment (15). This suggests that in clinical practice, when faced with children with recurrent hyperthermia and elevated inflammatory markers (e.g., PCT), we need to consider not only infectious diseases and common rheumatic immune diseases such as juvenile idiopathic arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus, but also the possibility of rare connective tissue diseases such as HA20 and genetic testing to help confirm the diagnosis if necessary.
107	
108	HA20 is a monogenic genetic disorder whose pathogenesis is mainly associated with a TNFAIP3 minus function mutation affecting A20, which is encoded by the TNFAIP3 gene, located on chromosome 6q23.3, and is a negative regulator of the tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-nuclear factor-κB signaling channel (16). A20 has an ovarian tumor region (OTU) structural domain in the N-terminal region, and a seven zinc finger (ZnF) structural domain in the C-terminal region. These two structural domains are negatively regulated by modification of the target proteins in the pathway. When the TNFAIP3 gene is mutated, A20 expression is reduced, the negative regulation of the TNF-nuclear factor-κB signaling channel is weakened, and NK-κB activation is increased, which in turn causes an increase in systemic inflammatory factors such as interleukin (IL)-1, IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α, and patients develop a systemic inflammatory response (17). In our case, IL-6, IL-4, and IL-10 all showed elevations, which is similar to previous studies. No pure mutations have been reported in HA20, and the mutation in this disease is usually an autosomal dominant heterozygous mutation. Mutations in the TNFAIP3 gene are widely distributed from the OTU to ZnF7 structural domains, with the OTU region and ZnF4 region being the most common, with a variety of mutations, including shift mutations, nonsense mutations, missense mutations, splice site mutations, and large deletions. The first two of which are more common in clinical practice (18). The patient in this case showed a shift mutation: TNFAIP3 (chr6:138197151): NM_006290.3:c.653del:p.Leu218TrpfsTer10, and this mutation has not been reported before.
109	
110	The clinical symptoms of HA20 are variable, including recurrent fever, recurrent oral and genital ulcers, rash, arthritis, and gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms. A small number of patients also develop neurological symptoms and cardiovascular lesions. Significantly different from Behçet’s disease, HA20 patients experience a significant increase in inflammatory factors, especially during relapses, along with low titers of autoantibodies. In contrast, HA20 patients often have a combination of autoimmune diseases, such as SLE and autoimmune thyroid disease (18). Some patients have a probability of having abnormalities in relevant tests even though they do not meet the diagnostic criteria for these immunological disorders. For example, the patient in the report had fluctuating presence of various autoantibodies such as antinuclear antibodies and anti-dsDNA (2). Similar to previous reports, this patient in our case presented with abnormalities in the indicators, including antinuclear antibodies, serum amyloid A protein, and anti-neutrophilic cytoplasmic antibodies. There was also an abnormality in the thyroid antibody test, which may be related to the patient's abnormal immune function. Non-autoimmune complications such as IgA vasculitis, chronic hepatitis, nephrotic syndrome, and Hodgkin's lymphoma also occur in the HA20 patient population. A small number of patients have been reported HA20 co-infection with Epstein–Barr virus (12, 19) that is similar to the child in this case report, but whether Epstein–Barr virus infection is associated with HA20 requires further study. Patients with HA20 also present with some immunodeficiency symptoms such as recurrent infections, hypogammaglobulinemia, low IgA and IgE, low IgG, and CD19 and CD4 cytopenias (19–21). In these respects, this patient in the study showed high IgE and IgA on admission and an increase in CD19 cells on examination, but showed a decrease in IgA on retesting 2 months later, which differs from previous reports. HA20 has an earlier age of onset in childhood, and most present with recurrent fever and significant elevation of inflammatory factors, more severe GI symptoms, and more common autoimmune disease (18). In addition, the patient in our case presented with an elevated anti-streptolysin O, which was not submitted in the previous report. Whether this abnormality is related to HA20 requires further study.
111	
112	The diagnosis of HA20 currently relies on whole exome sequencing. When patients present with recurrent fever, mouth ulcers, and genital ulcers, especially in the pediatric population, the possibility of HA20 needs to be considered. In the early stages of the disease, HA20 presents as recurrent mucosal ulcers and is therefore difficult to distinguish from diseases that also present as mucosal ulcers, such as Behcet's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, periodic fever with aphthous pharyngitis and adenitis, hyperimmunoglobulinemia D syndrome (HIDS), and inflammatory bowel disease (22). Whole exome sequencing of the ulcer helps clinicians to confirm the presence of the TNFAIP3 mutation and thus the diagnosis of HA20.
113	
114	There is no standard treatment protocol for HA20, and commonly used drugs include systemic glucocorticoids, immunosuppressive agents, and biologic agents. Most patients respond well to treatment with systemic glucocorticoids. Colchicine is often used clinically in the treatment of HA20. Other immunosuppressive agents include methotrexate, cyclosporine, thalidomide, sirolimus, and tacrolimus. Biologic agents include anti-TNF-α drugs, anti-IL-1 drugs, anti-IL-6 drugs, and JAK inhibitors (13, 18, 21). A few patients were in remission from HA20 hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, both autologous and allogeneic (3, 22). However, it has been reported that a child who underwent autologous stem cell transplantation relapsed after 18 months of remission and had to be re-treated with immunosuppressive drugs (9). Some patients with recurrent respiratory infections underwent tonsillectomy. In this study, the patient showed significant improvement in fever symptoms after taking prednisone, but the oral ulcers were not controlled. After further treatment with methotrexate and thalidomide, oral ulcers improved, and the infection indexes were reduced to normal on review, and after 10 months of follow-up and examination, the dose of prednisone was gradually being reduced and the patient's condition did not recur.
115	
116	In the face of patients with recurrent high fever with markedly elevated inflammatory factors, especially in younger pediatric patients like the one in this case, it is currently a challenge whether we can identify and diagnose HA20 in the early stages of its onset. Regarding the treatment of HA20, although the current multiple drug treatments and others can lead to remission, there is a lack of long-term follow-up data, and the long-term survival of patients needs further study.
